createProject.title: New project
createProject.name: Name
createProject.nameHelp: A label to recognize this project by — your company or website name. Only used inside OpenSEO, not shown publicly.
createProject.domainHelp: Your website's domain. Needed to connect Google Search Console, track rankings, and run a site audit — you can add it later if you don't have it handy now.
createProject.domainNote: You can connect Search Console and set up rank tracking after creating the project.
createProject.countryHelp: The country whose Google results and search volume this project focuses on. Affects keyword data, rankings and competitor comparisons.
createProject.languageHelp: The language keyword and search data is pulled in. Automatically matches the country you picked; only changeable when a country supports more than one.
createProject.marketNote: Keyword, SERP, and domain data uses this country and language unless a call asks for a different one. Change it later in project settings.

keywordResearch.modeHelp: How to expand your keyword: Auto picks the best method, Related finds similar terms, Suggestions mirrors Google's autocomplete, Ideas is broader topic exploration.
keywordResearch.resultsHelp: Maximum number of keywords to return per search.
keywordResearch.clickstreamHelp: Google reports one combined search volume for similar keywords (e.g. 'seo tool' and 'seo tools'). Turn this on to estimate each keyword's own volume. Costs 2x the credits.
keywordResearch.gadsNotice: Keyword data for this country comes from Google Ads — search volume, CPC, and trends are available, but difficulty and intent are not.

columns.volumeHelp: Estimated average monthly searches for this keyword.
columns.compHelp: Paid-search competition from Google Ads (0-1): higher means more advertisers bidding.
columns.scoreHelp: Organic ranking difficulty (0-100): higher means harder to reach Google's top 10.
columns.intentHelp: The likely reason behind the search: Informational (learning), Navigational (finding a site), Commercial (comparing), or Transactional (ready to buy/act).

desc.informational: The searcher wants information or answers. Use this for educational content, guides, and comparison-light explainers.
desc.commercial: The searcher is researching options before a purchase. Treat this as buying intent for comparisons, alternatives, and product-led pages.
desc.transactional: The searcher is ready to complete an action, often a purchase. Prioritize clear offers, pricing, trials, or conversion paths.
desc.navigational: The searcher is looking for a specific site, brand, or page. These queries usually reward matching the expected destination.
desc.unknown: Intent was not available for this keyword, so avoid making content strategy decisions from this badge alone.

guide.title: How to Get the Most Out of OpenSEO
guide.intro: A practical, priority-ordered guide to using this tool for real SEO results — not just clicking around.
guide.step1Body: Enter your real domain and pick the right country/language when creating a project — every number after this (rankings, volume, competitors) is scoped to this market. Getting this wrong quietly skews everything.
guide.step2Body: This is the single most valuable connection you can make. It gives you your *actual* clicks, impressions and average position from Google — data no keyword tool can estimate for you. Do this before anything else in Settings.
guide.step3Title: 3. Start keyword research broad, then narrow
guide.step3Body: Search a broad 'seed' keyword first (e.g. your main product/service). Use 'Ideas' mode to see the full landscape, then use filters (Volume, low Score = easier to rank, matching Intent) to find realistic opportunities — not just the highest-volume terms everyone else is chasing.
guide.step4Title: 4. Prioritize by Score vs Volume, not Volume alone
guide.step4Body: A keyword with 500 searches/month and Score 15 is usually a better target than one with 5,000 searches and Score 80 — especially for a new or small site. Low competition keywords compound: you rank faster, get real traffic sooner, and build authority to go after bigger terms later.
guide.step5Body: Informational keywords want a helpful guide/article. Commercial keywords want a comparison or 'best X' page. Transactional keywords want a product/service page with a clear call-to-action. Writing the wrong content type for the intent is why pages with 'good' keywords still don't rank or convert.
guide.step6Title: 6. Track rankings for keywords you actually target
guide.step6Body: Don't track everything — track the specific keywords you're writing content for or optimizing pages around. Rank Tracking tells you if your work is paying off over time; without it you're optimizing blind.
guide.step7Body: Backlinks remain one of Google's strongest ranking signals. Look up your own domain to see your current link profile, then look up a competitor ranking above you for the same keywords — their backlinks often explain the gap.
guide.step8Title: 8. Run a Site Audit before chasing new keywords
guide.step8Body: Technical problems (broken links, missing tags, slow pages) can hold back pages that would otherwise rank well. Fixing existing issues is often faster ROI than producing new content.
guide.step9Title: 9. Use Domain Overview to size up any market
guide.step9Body: Before investing heavily in a niche, look up the strongest domains in it. It tells you honestly whether you're entering an easy market or a crowded one — and who you're actually competing with.
guide.step10Title: 10. Check Brand Lookup and Prompt Explorer periodically
guide.step10Body: Increasingly, people find businesses through AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini) as well as Google. These tools show whether your brand shows up when AI answers relevant questions — a newer but fast-growing channel worth monitoring.
guide.closingBody: Research keywords → prioritize the realistic ones → publish content matched to intent → track rankings → fix technical issues → repeat. SEO compounds over months, not days — consistency beats intensity.
